medical.title: 'Just one more episode'? How to keep digital distractions from stealing your sleep
medical.summary: It's happened to us all: You're poised to go to sleep, but a "digital distraction" keeps you up hours later than planned.

medical.title: Anti-inflammatory peptide shows potential to prevent diabetes-related vision loss
medical.summary: According to a study published in October in the journal Biomedicine & Pharmacotherapy, a molecule naturally produced by the human body may help protect vision against damage caused by high blood sugar. This finding paves the way for new strategies to prevent diabetic retinopathy. This complication affects more than 22% of people with diabetes worldwide. It occurs when high blood sugar levels cause inflammation and damage neurons and blood vessels in the retina, which can lead to permanent vision loss.

medical.title: Nicotine and tobacco smoke damage cells involved in tissue repair
medical.summary: Nicotine pouches can expose the oral mucosa to high local concentrations of nicotine. A study by the University of Oulu shows that nicotine and tobacco smoke have harmful effects on cells that play a key role in tissue regeneration and wound healing. The findings, published in the Archives of Toxicology, shed light on how nicotine products may compromise oral health and the body's ability to repair damaged tissue.

medical.title: Improved blood test offers less invasive way to detect Alzheimer's disease
medical.summary: A new study in Nature Aging from Lund University in Sweden shows that improved blood tests for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease can now be used with accuracy similar to that of the cerebrospinal fluid tests that have long been the standard in health care. The blood test has been approved for use in Europe, the U.S. and Japan, among other places. The researchers hope that doctors will now gradually be able to use it more widely—and that, in many cases, patients will be able to avoid the more invasive cerebrospinal fluid test.

medical.title: Outside stressors for military members can cause more medical visits
medical.summary: A new University of Massachusetts Amherst and Naval Health Research Center–led study of more than 34,000 active-duty U.S. military members enrolled in the U.S. Millennium Cohort Study finds those dealing with stress beyond their roles in the service tend to utilize health care more often.

medical.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
medical.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

medical.title: How the brain builds the present through the lens of the past
medical.summary: Why does the same sensory stimulus sometimes feel different depending on what came before it? In a study published in Science Advances, a team of neuroscientists at SISSA-Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati has identified a neural mechanism that helps explain how recent experience shapes present perception: a frontal cortical area carries a memory trace of previous sensory events and combines it with current sensory input.

medical.title: Seasonal mass vaccination with R21 malaria vaccine effective in reducing malaria infection
medical.summary: Vaccinating whole communities with the malaria vaccine R21 before the rainy season, alongside existing malaria control tools, can reduce the odds of infection by up to 70%, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

medical.title: Where math and language meet: Brain scans reveal shared regions
medical.summary: Researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, are helping solve an ongoing debate in the field of neuroscience. Two contradictory positions assume that either math and language are processed in unique areas of the brain, or they are processed together somewhere. Their new research, published in the journal Science Advances, says both are correct in some way: While specialized regions do exist, so does a region newly identified as processing both math and language.

medical.title: 'We are finally listening to the experiences of autistic people'
medical.summary: Dr. Lonnie Zwaigenbaum uses the word "joy" a lot when he talks about autism.

medical.title: Lyme disease leaves lasting changes in bone marrow, study finds
medical.summary: A new study led by researchers at Tufts University School of Medicine suggests that infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, can leave lasting changes in the immune system, even after the infection is treated. The changes occur in the bone marrow, where many of the body's immune cells are made, potentially altering how the immune system responds to future threats.

medical.title: The child development 'sweet spot' that affects adult taste preference
medical.summary: A baby's transition from breast milk or formula to a range of solid foods is the likely "sweet spot" for introducing nutritional variety that influences lifelong taste preferences by rewiring circuits in the brain, new research in mice suggests.

medical.title: Targeting a cellular 'traffic jam' treats multiple diseases in mice
medical.summary: A single therapy may be able to treat inherited disorders of both the kidneys and eyes—and potentially more genetic diseases called proteinopathies, researchers at the Broad Institute have discovered.

medical.title: How does hormonal contraception affect well-being?
medical.summary: Millions of women use hormonal contraception—usually the contraceptive pill. In Germany, around one in four women between the ages of 18 and 49 takes it. At the same time, there is considerable scientific debate about the possible risks to mental health. Researchers at the Universities of Göttingen, Leipzig and Witten/Herdecke used long-term data to investigate whether hormonal contraception affects well-being. They analyzed data from over 5,200 women in Germany who were repeatedly surveyed over a period of up to 14 years.

medical.title: Adolescent and teen depression linked to heavier substance use
medical.summary: Adolescents and teenagers who drink more alcohol or use multiple forms of marijuana are much more likely to experience major depression. In addition, girls, older teens and multiracial teens are more likely to experience major depression, regardless of drug or alcohol use.

medical.title: Possible new treatment for Wilson disease seeks to minimize effects on mitochondria using metformin
medical.summary: Wilson disease is a rare genetic condition in which the liver loses the ability to effectively remove copper, allowing it to accumulate in the body. This toxic buildup affects the liver, brain, eyes and kidneys and is particularly bad for mitochondria, the cell's all-important power plants.

medical.title: The surprising cancer connection at the heart of Alzheimer's
medical.summary: People say "the body keeps score"—but it might be more accurate to say our neurons do. In healthy people, neurons accumulate about 17 single-nucleotide variants each year, a pattern that holds from birth through a person's final years, according to research from HHMI investigator Chris Walsh and others.

medical.title: Volunteering delivers purpose—but also anxiety
medical.summary: New research has found that people who volunteer have a greater purpose in life, but it comes at a cost, with volunteering also linked to higher levels of anxiety.

medical.title: Most people make a successful transition to adult life after being born prematurely
medical.summary: How do things go for people born with extremely low birth weight? A new Swedish study shows that most of them are leading independent lives, participate in work or education, and have established relationships by the time they reach their late 20s. At the same time, slightly fewer have moved out of their parents' home, entered the labor market or ever been in a romantic relationship compared with people born following a full-term pregnancy.

medical.title: New smartphone tool could help young people seek support for eating disorders earlier
medical.summary: Researchers have found that a smartphone-friendly digital tool designed to encourage help-seeking among young people with eating disorders is both feasible and acceptable, paving the way for a larger clinical trial.

medical.title: Researchers urge significant 'peacetime' investment in contact tracing apps and digital public health tools
medical.summary: Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, university researchers have detailed how public health agencies across the world can be better prepared for the next epidemic through effective deployment of Bluetooth contact tracing apps and related digital public health tools.

medical.title: Discovery points to new approach for treating diabetes—no insulin required
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown way the body's muscles absorb glucose from the blood—without insulin.

medical.title: Brain stacking: An expert weighs in on whether this TikTok trend can really boost your brainpower
medical.summary: Brain stacking is a new TikTok trend dedicated to making time for activities that engage our mind, such as reading or doing puzzles.

medical.title: Newly discovered mechanism may help ovarian cancer cells silence tumor-suppressor genes
medical.summary: Researchers at Umeå University have discovered how chemical marks on RNA control a DNA methylation enzyme and contribute to the silencing of tumor-suppressor genes in ovarian cancer cells. The findings provide new insights into the disease and may, in the long term, contribute to the development of new treatment strategies for high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

science.title: Fiona the hippo dies after failed effort to remove swallowed hat
science.summary: World-famous hippopotamus Fiona has died after several failed attempts by vets to remove a woolly hat that she accidentally swallowed, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday.

science.title: Nature's multilayered defenses against crop pests and viruses revealed
science.summary: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, in collaboration with Syngenta and Keele University, have discovered how a commercial barley hybrid uses three complementary natural defenses to protect itself against aphids and the damaging viruses they spread. The findings could help breeders develop crops with stronger natural protection against pests and diseases.

science.title: Data centers damage air quality long-distance, study reveals
science.summary: The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

science.title: The Stormy Southwest Pacific
science.summary: Tropical Cyclone Xavier launched the basin’s storm season with a bang.

science.title: computor: AI tutor as a programming learning aid
science.summary: Artificial intelligence is now capable of writing entire computer programs. This poses a challenge for university education. How can students still learn to program for themselves if an AI can do the work for them? Students should be able to use AI tools effectively, but they must also understand how programs work and how to troubleshoot errors. At the Institute of Theoretical and Computational Physics at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), a team led by Christopher Albert has developed the "computor" learning platform for this purpose. The system is already being used in teaching and is available to the public.

science.title: How nature-based solutions are failing informal settlements
science.summary: New research from UCT says nature-based solutions for climate adaptation must move beyond participation to power-sharing partnerships that recognize lived experiences and relationships with nature.

science.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
science.summary: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space.

science.title: Innovative technology offers a bold new vision for monitoring ocean health
science.summary: On an early October morning, as MBARI's research vessel Paragon left Moss Landing with three robots loaded on its deck, Monterey Bay was showing off.

science.title: New mondo grass species found in Yunnan
science.summary: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape.

science.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
science.summary: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name.

Today, there are at least 12 peacocks, including peahens roaming the area. “In the mornings and evenings, we hear their loud and piercing […]

environment.title: How one tiny island made conservation work
environment.summary: Out in the Bristol Channel, nestled between Wales and England, the rugged island of Lundy is one of the UK’s most pioneering conservation stories. Watch the full story.

environment.summary: JAKARTA — In Muncar, a busy fishing port on the southeastern coast of Indonesia’s East Java province, sharks can fetch as much as 1.5 million rupiah each, or about $82. However, their value to fishing communities comes at a cost to conservation: Threatened species, including the critically endangered scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), made up a […]

environment.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
environment.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

environment.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
environment.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

environment.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
environment.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

environment.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

environment.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
environment.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.

mix_items.title: Fiona the hippo dies after failed effort to remove swallowed hat
mix_items.summary: World-famous hippopotamus Fiona has died after several failed attempts by vets to remove a woolly hat that she accidentally swallowed, the Cincinnati Zoo announced Thursday.

mix_items.title: Nature's multilayered defenses against crop pests and viruses revealed
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, in collaboration with Syngenta and Keele University, have discovered how a commercial barley hybrid uses three complementary natural defenses to protect itself against aphids and the damaging viruses they spread. The findings could help breeders develop crops with stronger natural protection against pests and diseases.

mix_items.title: Data centers damage air quality long-distance, study reveals
mix_items.summary: The rapid expansion of data centers for artificial intelligence causes negative health and air quality impacts in regions far from where the brick-and-mortar facilities are located, according to a new study by MIT researchers.

mix_items.summary: Tropical Cyclone Xavier launched the basin’s storm season with a bang.

mix_items.title: computor: AI tutor as a programming learning aid
mix_items.summary: Artificial intelligence is now capable of writing entire computer programs. This poses a challenge for university education. How can students still learn to program for themselves if an AI can do the work for them? Students should be able to use AI tools effectively, but they must also understand how programs work and how to troubleshoot errors. At the Institute of Theoretical and Computational Physics at Graz University of Technology (TU Graz), a team led by Christopher Albert has developed the "computor" learning platform for this purpose. The system is already being used in teaching and is available to the public.

mix_items.title: How nature-based solutions are failing informal settlements
mix_items.summary: New research from UCT says nature-based solutions for climate adaptation must move beyond participation to power-sharing partnerships that recognize lived experiences and relationships with nature.

mix_items.title: Building structured-light systems in three dimensions
mix_items.summary: Structured light has become an important tool across modern optics. By shaping properties such as amplitude, phase, polarization and spatial mode, researchers can create light fields with capabilities beyond those of conventional laser beams. These engineered light fields are finding applications in communications, imaging, sensing, optical computing and quantum photonics. However, many structured-light systems still rely on multiple discrete optical components that require careful alignment and occupy significant space.

mix_items.title: Innovative technology offers a bold new vision for monitoring ocean health
mix_items.summary: On an early October morning, as MBARI's research vessel Paragon left Moss Landing with three robots loaded on its deck, Monterey Bay was showing off.

mix_items.title: New mondo grass species found in Yunnan
mix_items.summary: Botanists have described a new Ophiopogon species from the Yunnan Wenshan National Nature Reserve in southeastern China. They named it Ophiopogon longiscapus for its unusually long flowering stalk, or scape.

mix_items.title: Organizational science offers new lens for studying extremism
mix_items.summary: Accepting the Republican nomination for president in 1964, Barry Goldwater declared, "I would remind you that extremism in the defense of liberty is no vice!" His statement illustrates how the cause being defended can shape judgments about the actions taken in its name.

mix_items.title: 'Just one more episode'? How to keep digital distractions from stealing your sleep
mix_items.summary: It's happened to us all: You're poised to go to sleep, but a "digital distraction" keeps you up hours later than planned.

mix_items.title: Anti-inflammatory peptide shows potential to prevent diabetes-related vision loss
mix_items.summary: According to a study published in October in the journal Biomedicine & Pharmacotherapy, a molecule naturally produced by the human body may help protect vision against damage caused by high blood sugar. This finding paves the way for new strategies to prevent diabetic retinopathy. This complication affects more than 22% of people with diabetes worldwide. It occurs when high blood sugar levels cause inflammation and damage neurons and blood vessels in the retina, which can lead to permanent vision loss.

mix_items.title: Nicotine and tobacco smoke damage cells involved in tissue repair
mix_items.summary: Nicotine pouches can expose the oral mucosa to high local concentrations of nicotine. A study by the University of Oulu shows that nicotine and tobacco smoke have harmful effects on cells that play a key role in tissue regeneration and wound healing. The findings, published in the Archives of Toxicology, shed light on how nicotine products may compromise oral health and the body's ability to repair damaged tissue.

mix_items.title: Improved blood test offers less invasive way to detect Alzheimer's disease
mix_items.summary: A new study in Nature Aging from Lund University in Sweden shows that improved blood tests for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's disease can now be used with accuracy similar to that of the cerebrospinal fluid tests that have long been the standard in health care. The blood test has been approved for use in Europe, the U.S. and Japan, among other places. The researchers hope that doctors will now gradually be able to use it more widely—and that, in many cases, patients will be able to avoid the more invasive cerebrospinal fluid test.

mix_items.title: Outside stressors for military members can cause more medical visits
mix_items.summary: A new University of Massachusetts Amherst and Naval Health Research Center–led study of more than 34,000 active-duty U.S. military members enrolled in the U.S. Millennium Cohort Study finds those dealing with stress beyond their roles in the service tend to utilize health care more often.

mix_items.title: Experimental compound burns fat without sacrificing muscle
mix_items.summary: Researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a compound that could transform weight-loss treatment by helping the body burn more energy instead of suppressing appetite like Ozempic and Wegovy. In mice, the compound boosted energy expenditure by up to 18%, improved blood sugar control, reduced liver fat, and promoted weight loss without significant muscle loss. Even more promising, combining it with existing GLP-1 medications produced greater benefits than either treatment alone.

mix_items.title: How the brain builds the present through the lens of the past
mix_items.summary: Why does the same sensory stimulus sometimes feel different depending on what came before it? In a study published in Science Advances, a team of neuroscientists at SISSA-Scuola Internazionale Superiore di Studi Avanzati has identified a neural mechanism that helps explain how recent experience shapes present perception: a frontal cortical area carries a memory trace of previous sensory events and combines it with current sensory input.

mix_items.title: Seasonal mass vaccination with R21 malaria vaccine effective in reducing malaria infection
mix_items.summary: Vaccinating whole communities with the malaria vaccine R21 before the rainy season, alongside existing malaria control tools, can reduce the odds of infection by up to 70%, according to a new study published in The Lancet.

mix_items.title: Where math and language meet: Brain scans reveal shared regions
mix_items.summary: Researchers, including those at the University of Tokyo, are helping solve an ongoing debate in the field of neuroscience. Two contradictory positions assume that either math and language are processed in unique areas of the brain, or they are processed together somewhere. Their new research, published in the journal Science Advances, says both are correct in some way: While specialized regions do exist, so does a region newly identified as processing both math and language.

mix_items.title: 'We are finally listening to the experiences of autistic people'
mix_items.summary: Dr. Lonnie Zwaigenbaum uses the word "joy" a lot when he talks about autism.

mix_items.title: Lyme disease leaves lasting changes in bone marrow, study finds
mix_items.summary: A new study led by researchers at Tufts University School of Medicine suggests that infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, can leave lasting changes in the immune system, even after the infection is treated. The changes occur in the bone marrow, where many of the body's immune cells are made, potentially altering how the immune system responds to future threats.

mix_items.title: The child development 'sweet spot' that affects adult taste preference
mix_items.summary: A baby's transition from breast milk or formula to a range of solid foods is the likely "sweet spot" for introducing nutritional variety that influences lifelong taste preferences by rewiring circuits in the brain, new research in mice suggests.

mix_items.title: Targeting a cellular 'traffic jam' treats multiple diseases in mice
mix_items.summary: A single therapy may be able to treat inherited disorders of both the kidneys and eyes—and potentially more genetic diseases called proteinopathies, researchers at the Broad Institute have discovered.

mix_items.title: How does hormonal contraception affect well-being?
mix_items.summary: Millions of women use hormonal contraception—usually the contraceptive pill. In Germany, around one in four women between the ages of 18 and 49 takes it. At the same time, there is considerable scientific debate about the possible risks to mental health. Researchers at the Universities of Göttingen, Leipzig and Witten/Herdecke used long-term data to investigate whether hormonal contraception affects well-being. They analyzed data from over 5,200 women in Germany who were repeatedly surveyed over a period of up to 14 years.

mix_items.title: Adolescent and teen depression linked to heavier substance use
mix_items.summary: Adolescents and teenagers who drink more alcohol or use multiple forms of marijuana are much more likely to experience major depression. In addition, girls, older teens and multiracial teens are more likely to experience major depression, regardless of drug or alcohol use.

mix_items.title: Possible new treatment for Wilson disease seeks to minimize effects on mitochondria using metformin
mix_items.summary: Wilson disease is a rare genetic condition in which the liver loses the ability to effectively remove copper, allowing it to accumulate in the body. This toxic buildup affects the liver, brain, eyes and kidneys and is particularly bad for mitochondria, the cell's all-important power plants.

mix_items.title: The surprising cancer connection at the heart of Alzheimer's
mix_items.summary: People say "the body keeps score"—but it might be more accurate to say our neurons do. In healthy people, neurons accumulate about 17 single-nucleotide variants each year, a pattern that holds from birth through a person's final years, according to research from HHMI investigator Chris Walsh and others.

mix_items.title: Volunteering delivers purpose—but also anxiety
mix_items.summary: New research has found that people who volunteer have a greater purpose in life, but it comes at a cost, with volunteering also linked to higher levels of anxiety.

mix_items.title: Most people make a successful transition to adult life after being born prematurely
mix_items.summary: How do things go for people born with extremely low birth weight? A new Swedish study shows that most of them are leading independent lives, participate in work or education, and have established relationships by the time they reach their late 20s. At the same time, slightly fewer have moved out of their parents' home, entered the labor market or ever been in a romantic relationship compared with people born following a full-term pregnancy.

mix_items.title: New smartphone tool could help young people seek support for eating disorders earlier
mix_items.summary: Researchers have found that a smartphone-friendly digital tool designed to encourage help-seeking among young people with eating disorders is both feasible and acceptable, paving the way for a larger clinical trial.

mix_items.title: Researchers urge significant 'peacetime' investment in contact tracing apps and digital public health tools
mix_items.summary: Drawing on lessons from the COVID-19 pandemic, university researchers have detailed how public health agencies across the world can be better prepared for the next epidemic through effective deployment of Bluetooth contact tracing apps and related digital public health tools.

mix_items.title: Discovery points to new approach for treating diabetes—no insulin required
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Cincinnati College of Medicine have identified a previously unknown way the body's muscles absorb glucose from the blood—without insulin.

mix_items.title: Brain stacking: An expert weighs in on whether this TikTok trend can really boost your brainpower
mix_items.summary: Brain stacking is a new TikTok trend dedicated to making time for activities that engage our mind, such as reading or doing puzzles.

mix_items.title: Newly discovered mechanism may help ovarian cancer cells silence tumor-suppressor genes
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Umeå University have discovered how chemical marks on RNA control a DNA methylation enzyme and contribute to the silencing of tumor-suppressor genes in ovarian cancer cells. The findings provide new insights into the disease and may, in the long term, contribute to the development of new treatment strategies for high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma.

Today, there are at least 12 peacocks, including peahens roaming the area. “In the mornings and evenings, we hear their loud and piercing […]

mix_items.title: How one tiny island made conservation work
mix_items.summary: Out in the Bristol Channel, nestled between Wales and England, the rugged island of Lundy is one of the UK’s most pioneering conservation stories. Watch the full story.

mix_items.summary: A small team of scientists was counting plants for a forest census near Manaus in northern Brazil when fire season started in October 2023. Some days the smoke was too thick to see; on other days it was too hot to wear conventional masks, so Aretha Guimarães, a biologist with Brazil’s National Institute of Amazonian […]

mix_items.title: Threatened species make up half of shark catches at Indonesian fishing port, study finds
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — In Muncar, a busy fishing port on the southeastern coast of Indonesia’s East Java province, sharks can fetch as much as 1.5 million rupiah each, or about $82. However, their value to fishing communities comes at a cost to conservation: Threatened species, including the critically endangered scalloped hammerhead (Sphyrna lewini), made up a […]

mix_items.title: Antarctica’s ice cliffs are collapsing faster than expected, but there’s a twist
mix_items.summary: A surprising new study suggests Antarctica's towering ice cliffs may be less vulnerable to catastrophic collapse than scientists once feared. After tracking more than 15,000 ice cliffs, researchers discovered that even the tallest cliffs, which can collapse at alarming speeds, often stabilize rather than triggering an unstoppable chain reaction. Underwater ridges, surrounding water, and broken ice appear to provide natural defenses against further collapse.

mix_items.title: Scientists discover a surprisingly simple way to turn coffee waste into fuel
mix_items.summary: Scientists have developed an efficient method to transform used coffee grounds into a potential source of biodiesel while preserving the leftover material for other renewable fuels and valuable chemicals. The discovery could turn millions of tons of discarded coffee waste into a surprisingly useful resource for sustainable energy.

mix_items.title: DNA on the Shroud of Turin reveals centuries of hidden secrets
mix_items.summary: The Shroud of Turin, one of history's most mysterious religious artifacts, is yielding surprising new clues through DNA analysis. Scientists have uncovered a complex mixture of biological traces that may reveal more about the cloth's past and the environments it encountered. The findings offer a fresh scientific perspective on a centuries-old mystery that continues to spark fascination and debate.

mix_items.title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

mix_items.title: An ancient ocean full of giant predators reveals a surprising twist in evolution
mix_items.summary: A remarkable fossil discovery in Colombia is challenging how scientists understand major evolutionary changes in Earth's history. Researchers uncovered an incredibly diverse ancient marine ecosystem where giant reptiles, sharks, and other creatures thrived as older evolutionary groups approached extinction and newer ones emerged. They call this previously unrecognized pattern a "Biotic Inflection," suggesting that major transformations in life can occur without mass extinctions.
